#Part 1 — Reconstruct (roughly 1–2 paragraphs plus code)
#Pull the ACS data the article appears to rely on. Document:

#Which variable(s) you used and why. Include the variable code.

Variables Used

B17001_001E : total population for whom poverty status is determined - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Using *B01003_001E : total population* would not be accurate because the ACS excludes some people from their poverty rate calculation if they are determined inapplicable. 

B17001_002E : total population below the poverty level - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Dividing the total population below the poverty level by the total population applicable will give me the poverty rate. 

B17001_001M : MOE for the total - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainity of the statistical outcome.

B17001_002M : MOE for below poverty - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainty of the statistical outcome. 

#Which years and survey (acs5 vs acs1) you used and why.

I am used the 2006-2010 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2010 data mentioned in the article, and the 2013-2017 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2017 data mentioned in the article. Although the article mentions some data from the 2016 ACS1 report, it's main claim compares the change in the poverty rate from 2010 to 2017. 

#What you had to assume, because the article does not say.

I assumed that the article correctly calculated the poverty rate by using "total population for whom poverty status is determined" rather than just "total population". I myself did not realize that this is the correct way to calculate the poverty rate before reading this on the US Census Bureau website. 

#State clearly whether the two periods the article compares overlap. If they do, say what that means for any conclusion drawn from the comparison.

No, the two periods do not overlap.  

#Part 2 — Test (code plus interpretation)
#For each tract:

#Data set up

library (tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)

vars <- (
total = "B17001_001",
below = "B17001_002"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output ="wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

#Compute the poverty rate (or whatever variable you are using if you found your own article) and its margin of error. Use moe_prop() — a rate is a proportion, and the MOE does not carry over from the count.

#poverty rate
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)

#margin of error 
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))

acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))

# ============================================================
# FIGURE 2
# Distribution of Poverty Rates: 2010 vs. 2017
# ============================================================

poverty_long <- poverty_change |>
  select(
    GEOID,
    poverty_rt_2010,
    poverty_rt_2017
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(poverty_rt_2010, poverty_rt_2017),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "poverty_rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = recode(
      year,
      poverty_rt_2010 = "2010",
      poverty_rt_2017 = "2017"
    ),
    poverty_rate = poverty_rate * 100
  )

figure_2 <- ggplot(
  poverty_long,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = poverty_rate,
    fill = year
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.75,
    width = 0.6,
    outlier.alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Philadelphia Census Tract Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "Comparison of ACS 5-Year estimates for 2010 and 2017",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Poverty rate (%)",
    fill = "Period",
    caption = paste(
      "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates.",
      "Poverty rate = population below poverty level /",
      "population for whom poverty status is determined."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

figure_2


#Compute the coefficient of variation
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)

#flag reliability using the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.
reliability_table_2010 <- acs_2010 |> 
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ NA_character_,
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ NA_character_,
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

reliability_table_2017 <- acs_2017 |> 
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ NA_character_,
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ NA_character_,
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )
  
#Compute the change between the two periods and the margin of error of that change.

poverty_change <- acs_2010 |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME, poverty_rt_2010 = poverty_rt, poverty_moe_2010 = poverty_moe) |> 
  left_join( acs_2017 |> 
  select(GEOID, poverty_rt_2017 = poverty_rt, poverty_moe_2017 = poverty_moe),
  by = "GEOID")
  
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
  mutate(poverty_change = poverty_rt_2017 - poverty_rt_2010)
  
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
mutate(
  se_2010 = poverty_moe_2010 / 1.645,
  se_2017 = poverty_moe_2017 / 1.645,
  se_change = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
  change_moe = 1.645 * se_change
)
  
head(poverty_change)

library(gt)
library(scales)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# FIGURE 1
# Change in poverty rate with 90% margin of error
# ------------------------------------------------------------

error_bar_data <- poverty_change |>
  filter(
    !is.na(poverty_change),
    !is.na(change_moe)
  ) |>
  arrange(poverty_change) |>
  mutate(
    tract_order = row_number()
  )

figure_1 <- ggplot(
  error_bar_data,
  aes(
    x = tract_order,
    y = poverty_change * 100
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = (poverty_change - change_moe) * 100,
      ymax = (poverty_change + change_moe) * 100
    ),
    width = 0,
    alpha = 0.35,
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.7,
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in Poverty Rates Across Philadelphia Census Tracts",
    subtitle = "2017 minus 2010 poverty rate; points show estimates and bars show 90% margins of error",
    x = "Philadelphia census tracts, ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 5-Year Estimates (2006–2010 and 2013–2017)."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

figure_1


#Test whether the change is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence.

poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
  mutate(
  lower = poverty_change - change_moe,
  upper = poverty_change + change_moe,
  significant_90 = lower > 0 | upper < 0
)

#Report how many tracts show a statistically detectable change and how many do not.

table(poverty_change$significant_90)

FALSE: 313
There are 313 tracts without statistically detectable change.

TRUE: 63
There are 63 tracts with statistically detectable change. 

#Handle your missing values deliberately. Some tracts will produce NA. Find out why before you decide what to do about them, and say what you decided and why (often areas of no population like airports)

poverty_change |> 
  filter(is.na(significant_90)) |>

largely claims based on anecdotal evidence. When placed next to census data it appears that the claims are being backed by statistical analysis when they are not. The article actually admits to potential lack of evidence in the data but then proceeds to structure the article in this way anyway.
